title: What a Test Paper Can't Tell You
author: 100 Assessment
summary: This article distinguishes between assessment-for-summary and assessment-for-diagnosis, arguing that most school tests are built for the former but routinely misused for the latter. A test produces a score that answers 'how much has this pupil learned overall?'—analogous to a temperature reading. A diagnosis answers a different question: 'what, precisely, does this pupil understand and misunderstand, and what should they work on next?' These two goals pull test design in opposite directions, making them nearly incompatible in a single instrument. The article identifies three reasons Question Level Analysis (QLA) consistently disappoints: wrong answers don't reveal why (most exam questions test multiple things simultaneously, making wrong answers uninterpretable); two or three questions on any topic are statistically too few (noise swamps signal); and the questions sampled represent only a handful of footholds in a much larger curriculum domain. A genuine diagnostic question, by contrast, tests one thing in the plainest possible form—and in multiple-choice format, each distractor is deliberately designed to correspond to a specific identifiable misconception, making wrong answers informative rather than mute.
points: * Test and diagnostic are fundamentally different instruments built for different purposes: a summary test spreads pupils out and covers broad ground; a diagnostic isolates one idea and reveals the reason behind a wrong answer. * Most exam questions bundle multiple skills into one item, making wrong answers nearly uninterpretable for diagnostic purposes—a complex fractions question can be failed for four different unrelated reasons. * Two or three questions on any topic is statistically insufficient for individual-level conclusions: guessing, misreading, and random slippage swamp the signal from such a small sample. * The questions on any test sample only a handful of footholds in a large curriculum domain—getting fractions wrong on three questions doesn't reveal where in the broad fractions landscape the gap lies. * A true diagnostic question is stripped back to test one idea, with each multiple-choice distractor deliberately designed to correspond to a specific known misconception, making errors informative rather than mute.
quotes: A test score is a temperature reading. It tells you something is off without telling you what.
The problem is that the test paper was never built to answer the question Priya is now asking of it.

A summary test wants questions that spread pupils out and cover a lot of ground quickly. A diagnostic wants questions that isolate one idea at a time and reveal the reason behind a wrong answer. You cannot usually get both from the same paper.
So when Jack gets it wrong, what have we learned? Almost nothing we can act on. Was it the reading? The common denominator? A careless slip in the arithmetic? 'Wrong' is mute about the cause.
Three questions are a keyhole, not a window.
